study.title: Micah 3 Unrighteous leaders, corrupt prophets, and judgment on Zion
study.overview: Micah 3 presents a severe denunciation of the civil, religious and prophetic leadership of Israel and Judah. The prophet exposes the contrast between the duty of these leaders and the way they exploited the people, sold their word and distorted justice. The chapter culminates in such a heavy judgment of judgment that Jerusalem would be reduced to ruins, as a plowed field and as a desolate place.

outline.title: Responsible for justice, but devouring people
outline.explanation: Micah calls the leaders of Jacob and the rulers of Israel to the responsibility for knowing what is right. Instead, they hate good, love evil and treat the people as prey. The result will be that when they cry to the Lord they will receive no answer, because their violence has become a reason for judgment.

outline.title: Prophets who please those who feed them
outline.explanation: The prophet denounces the false messengers who proclaim peace or war as they receive sustenance. They will lose light, direction and credibility: the night will come upon their visions, their words will be silent, and will be ashamed because God will not answer them.

outline.title: The true prophet speaks by the Spirit, not out of interest
outline.explanation: In contrast to the false prophets, Micah declares to be filled with power, judgment, and strength of the Spirit of the Lord to proclaim the sin of Jacob and Israel. He accuses leaders, priests and prophets of building Zion with blood, bribery and wages, while they deceive themselves by thinking that God's presence the bookstore of evil.

outline.title: Zion will be devastated
outline.explanation: The chapter ends with the sentence: because of the corruption of their leaders, Zion will be pished as a field, Jerusalem will turn a mountain of ruins, and the mount of the temple will be like an area of forest. The image communicates total destruction and national humiliation.

study.context: The chapter speaks to civil, religious and prophetic leaders of Israel and Judah, showing that they had special responsibility before God. The commentator notes highlight that Micah confronts both political and religious leadership, and that the ruin of Jerusalem is presented as a direct consequence of moral and spiritual corruption. It is also mentioned that this judgment was later cited by Jeremiah, which shows the strength and continuity of this prophetic warning.
study.theology: Micah 3 teaches that authority without justice becomes aggravated guilt. God does not accept leadership that uses the people as a means of profit, nor worship used to cover up injustice. There is a strong theology of responsibility here: those who have received more light and more burden responds more seriously. The chapter also distinguishes the true word from the word bought: the faithful prophet speaks by impulse and commission of God, not to please people. Finally, divine judgment is not arbitrary; it responds to an entire structure of sin, in which rulers, priests and prophets rely mutually on corruption. The presence of the Lord is not amulet against discipline, but a holy reality that judges perversion.

scholarViews.insight: The leaders were morally responsible for the welfare of the people, and therefore their guilt was aggravated when they abused the office and destroyed Israel.
Micah speaks with courage because he has received commission and impulse from God; his denunciation is not born of himself, but from a higher order that sustains him.
The sentence of Zion describes a total destruction, in which the city would be demoted ruin and desolation as a sign of irreparable judgment.

questions: In what ways can a person use religious, political, or family authority to serve himself rather than serve others?
How to discern between a word that seeks to please people and a word that is born of fidelity to God?
In which areas can trust in God's presence come to an excuse to tolerate sin and injustice?
study.practice: Examine your responsibility before God where you exert influence, albeit small. Confess any selfish use of power, word, or position. If you teach, lead or advise, speak with truth and without hidden interest. If you are under leadership, pray for integrity in those who govern and refuse to participate in systems that reward corruption. Seek to align your life with righteousness, transparency and fear of the Lord, remembering that God does not approve of devotion without righteousness.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided are summarized and in English; therefore, some interpretative details were synthesized with caution, without adding information not present in them. The chapter does not in itself inform dates, specific political contexts or detailed identification of historical events, so such points have not been inferred beyond what the notes allowed.
